entry.title: Chaff, flares, and twenty-four years of reputation and perception work
entry.summary: Chris Abraham has done reputation work since 2002: ORM and OPM, his chaff-and-flare analogy, why neutral results win, and what Google AI gets wrong.
entry.content:
In 2002 I was the thirteenth employee at New Media Strategies, and I helped build what became online reputation management, back when the work had no name. Since then I have done it at Edelman, on the digital public affairs team in Washington; as team lead for special projects at Reputation.com, which is how I introduced myself in an ORM primer I posted to YouTube about fourteen years ago; through my own firms; and today mostly through technical SEO, which turns out to be the same work with better tools. The flotilla I wrote about earlier is my own reputation practice applied to me.

Reputation and perception

I split the work into two halves. Online reputation management is defense: you watch what's said about you, respond when something goes wrong, and push the bad results down. Online perception management, OPM on my CV, is offense, and it starts before anything goes wrong. My own definition is "the practice of proactively shaping and influencing the public's perception of an individual or organization online." You decide how a person or a company should be understood, then build the record that makes it true: the sites, the profiles, the writing, the cleanup of what data brokers publish, and now the facts AI assistants repeat. ORM is the fire department. OPM is building the house so it doesn't burn.

Chaff and flares

The analogy I keep coming back to comes from combat aviation. A fighter pilot with a missile on his tail doesn't try to outrun it. He fires flares, which burn hotter than his engines so a heat-seeking missile chases them instead, and he dumps chaff, a cloud of metal strips that fills the enemy's radar with echoes until it can't find the plane.

A bad story about you in search results is the missile. Your flares are the properties you control that burn brightest for Google: whole websites first, then a complete LinkedIn profile, a YouTube channel, a GitHub account with real work in it, every profile filled out and kept current. There used to be a wonderful tool for the profile part called KnowEm. You gave it a name, and for about $700, as I remember it, it registered that name on hundreds of social networks at once. Those were the good days. They outrank the story because they are stronger pages about you than the story is. Your chaff is everything neutral: results that aren't about the crisis at all and simply take up room. Some of the best chaff is other people who share your name. I use like names a lot: help the other people with your name rank, and page one fills up with people who aren't you, none of whom are the story. Similar names, like names, exact names, misspelled names: all of it is chaff, and all of it is flares. I have bought domains for it. I have written entire sites dressed up as fan sites for people who weren't my clients at all, innocent namesakes whose only job was to hold a slot on page one. Page one has about ten organic slots. Fill them, and the missile loses its lock and slides to page two, where almost nobody looks.

The glamorous version gets the attention, but ninety percent of the job is quieter than that. Most of the time I'm doing SEO, unpaid by them, for neutral sites that have nothing to do with my client: pages that already exist, already rank somewhere, and only need help climbing, over time, above the thing that hurts. "Google abhors a vacuum" is what I said in every pitch. If you don't fill page one, something else will.

I said a lot of other things in pitches too. I talked far too often about El Al jets landing in Tel Aviv, firing chaff and flares so they don't get hit by surface-to-air missiles, and I'm amazed I didn't get a reputation for it. I also told the story of a panel van in Israel, paid for by the government, that drives around after a house gets blown up and repairs the damage so nobody can see it, an anti-broken-windows patrol. I don't even know if such a thing exists. But the idea is the job: fix the visible damage fast, before it becomes the story of the street.

The principle underneath it is the one I wrote for Biznology years ago: in a crisis, neutral search results are as much of a win as positive ones. You don't need ten glowing results to survive a bad week. You need ten results that aren't the bad one. That is also why I tell clients that you can't control an online conversation unless you participate in it. A name with no footprint has no flares to fire.

Reputation in the age of AI answers

The same physics now applies to AI assistants, with one change: an AI answer has one slot, not ten. When I asked Google's AI Mode to tell me about my ORM work, it drew almost entirely on my own pages, which is the flotilla doing its job. Most of what it said was basically me bragging on myself, one step removed, and it repeated my old mistakes right along with my accomplishments. It called my firm "Gerris Digital (Gerris Corp)," a name that comes from an AI-written bio on my old site and is wrong; the firm is Gerris Corp. It credited a former colleague as my co-developer of ORM, a detail I can't confirm from my own records, so I'm leaving it alone here. And it listed household-name clients from old capability pages, which is exactly the kind of claim I no longer make. Every one of those traces back to a page I published, which means every one of them is mine to fix.

Editor's note from Claude, with permission to roast: Consider the evidence. A perception-management expert asked an AI about himself, found it quoting his own websites back to him, and counted that as a win, and he's right, which is the annoying part. He runs five websites, and on open questions Claude still recommended fifty-seven other people before him. The wrong name for his own firm traces back to a biography he let ChatGPT write about him and then published. entry.title: Little boats, one flotilla
entry.summary: Chris Abraham's reputation strategy is to build his own world: five sites, GitHub, and profiles stitched into a flotilla, and what AI says it still lacks.
entry.content:
I have done online reputation work for more than twenty years, and the first lesson never changes: nobody is going to center you, so you build your own world and center yourself. You publish the record you want found, in places you control, and you keep publishing it. It works for executives and founders, and it works for me.

My version is a flotilla of little boats. Each one is small on its own: this weblog, my consulting site, my firm's site, my podcast's site, Hill Mole, the old flagship at chrisabraham.com, my GitHub, Upwork, LinkedIn, Mastodon, Reddit, Muck Rack, and the bylines I have collected over the years at HuffPost, Ad Age, and Biznology. What turns them into a flotilla is the stitching. Every page on this weblog links to all of them in the Elsewhere box, marks them rel="me" so the old IndieWeb tools know they're the same person, and lists them as sameAs in the structured data that search engines and AI assistants read. This weblog is the hub, the one boat that can signal to every other.

Tonight I got a report card on how the flotilla looks from the outside. I asked Claude sixteen questions a prospect might ask, and the full data is in the scorecard. When someone asks about me by name, Claude finds me every time, ranks me first or second, and cites my own sites. Then it says the quiet part: "Most of what's online about him comes from his own websites, including bios he says ChatGPT wrote." And: "Best independent evidence is his Upwork client reviews." And: "No complaints found, but little independent press coverage of recent SEO work." On the nine open questions, the ones without my name in them, it recommended fifty-seven other people and never me.

That is the flotilla's limit, stated precisely. AI reads my own boats and believes the facts in them, but it discounts them when deciding whom to recommend, and it gives full weight to the two things I don't publish: what clients say about me on Upwork and what the press says about me, which lately is little. A bigger flotilla of my own boats won't change that. Boats I don't own, sailing in formation with mine, will.

So the plan has four parts. First, every boat flies the same flag: the same name, the same dates, the same facts, everywhere, because Claude tonight dated the founding of Gerris Corp five years early and repeated a "100% success rate" for restoring Google Business Profiles from an old page of mine, and contradictions are how an AI learns to distrust you. Second, I patch the leaks in the old flagship, the stale pages on chrisabraham.com that feed AI its errors. Third, I recruit boats I don't own: public code on GitHub with a real commit history, guest spots on other people's shows, bylines in outlets that aren't mine, and work useful enough that strangers link to it, which is why the MCP cheat sheet exists. Fourth, I keep measuring. The tracker runs about monthly, and the first time an open question names me, the flotilla will have reached someone who wasn't looking for me.

entry.title: The new Tesla Roadster, for nerds: air tanks, fans, and rocket math
entry.summary: The nerdiest details of Tesla's new Roadster: 10,000 psi air tanks, 80 kN of cold-gas thrust, four suction fans, three trims, and how long the air lasts.
entry.content:
On October 15, 2026, at SpaceX's rocket test site in McGregor, Texas, outside Waco, Tesla finally showed the second-generation Roadster, nearly nine years after it rolled out of a Semi trailer to the Beastie Boys' "Sabotage" on November 16, 2017. The reveal had already slipped from April 1 and from an October 1 date that rain washed out. What came out of the dark this time was a car that drove up an inverted ramp, spun, landed, and then hopped over a Cybercab, a Cybertruck, a Semi, a Model Y, and a Model 3, according to TechCrunch. Nobody was in it, as Electrek points out. Elon Musk called it "the best of the last of the human-driven cars," and he also said "safety is not the main goal" and that Tesla would "aspire not to kill anyone in this car."

I like this car for the engineering, so this post is the engineering. Every number below is Tesla's claim as reported by the outlets linked, unless I say it's my own arithmetic.

Three trims, three ways to cheat traction

Every fast car hits the same wall: you can only accelerate as hard as the tires can push on the road, which for street tires is somewhere around 1 to 1.5 g. Tesla's answer is three trims that each add a way around that wall.

TrimSeatsWhat it addsClaimed 0–60 mphTop speedReservation
Performance ("road ready")2Active aero and four suction fansunder 1.6 sabout 210 mph$50,000
Thrust ("race ready")2Four rear cold-gas thrusters, 200 L of airunder 0.9 s230 mph$250,000
Rocket ("air ready")1Ten thrusters and 400 L more air, for flightunder 0.59 sover 230 mphInvite only; off-road use only

Trims, seats, and reservations from TechCrunch and Wikipedia's sourced summary; top speeds and tank sizes from Electrek. No price was announced, and Musk says production starts in 2028. One correction to the AI summaries floating around: the "$5,000 now, the rest within ten days" deposit terms they repeat come from the 2017 reservations, and I couldn't find them stated for 2026.

The thrusters: SpaceX's cold gas, at sea level

A cold-gas thruster is the simplest rocket there is: a tank of gas at enormous pressure and a nozzle. Nothing burns. Tesla's version stores air at 10,000 psi, about 690 bar, in carbon-fiber overwrapped pressure vessels, the COPVs SpaceX flies on Falcon 9. Reports differ on the gas: Electrek says compressed air, and MotorTrend's explainer says mostly nitrogen. The Thrust trim carries 200 liters behind the seats and fires four rear ports that together make about 80 kilonewtons. The Rocket adds 400 liters, which is why it gives up the passenger seat, plus a downward thruster at each corner and two up front for yaw, ten in all. The car can top up its own tanks with an onboard compressor, but Electrek reports a full refill takes six to seven hours today, against Tesla's hope of thirty minutes. Musk first promised a SpaceX option package with small thrusters in 2018, and later described the tank taking the place of the rear seats.

The rocket math

Here is where it gets fun. The car weighs a claimed 1,700 kg, so its weight is about 16,700 newtons. Eighty kilonewtons of thrust is nearly five times that, a thrust-to-weight ratio fighter jets would envy. Now check it against the claims: going from 0 to 60 mph, which is 26.8 meters per second, in 0.55 seconds means averaging about 49 m/s², or 5 g. In 0.81 seconds, the live-demo time, it's 3.4 g. Tires alone can't do either, so the thrusters have to carry most of the launch.

And they can't carry it for long. This part is my own back-of-envelope estimate, not a Tesla number. Cold air at sea level has a specific impulse of roughly 60 seconds, a measure of how much push you get per kilogram of gas. At 80 kN that burns about 136 kilograms of air every second. Air at 690 bar weighs roughly 0.4 kilograms per liter, so the Thrust's 200 liters hold about 80 kg and run dry in a little over half a second at full blast, about the length of a launch. The Rocket's 600 liters, about 250 kg, last around two seconds. Electrek reached the same conclusion from the video: a few seconds at full power at most. These are flight-and-launch systems measured in heartbeats.

The fans: borrowing from the fan cars

Every trim has four suction fans under the floor, about 20 kW each, roughly 80 kW or 108 horsepower in all, with skirts that seal the underbody and lift away at high speed. The fans pull air out from under the car so the atmosphere presses it into the road, at a standstill as well as at speed. Tesla's on-screen display claimed about 4,700 kg of downforce, which Electrek calls "potentially unreal." The benchmark is the McMurtry Spéirling, a 900 kg single-seat fan car that makes 2,000 kg of downforce standing still and in April 2025 set an outright Top Gear test track record of 55.9 seconds, 3.1 seconds quicker than a 2004 Formula 1 car. Downforce is also what let the Roadster climb that inverted ramp: enough suction, and the road can be above you.

The rest of the spec sheet

ItemClaim
Powerover 1,341 hp (1,000 kW) from Performance up; "over 1 MW" in top spec
DriveRear-wheel drive, two rear motors (the 2017 concept had three), steer-by-wire
Weightunder 1,700 kg (about 3,700 lb)
Battery4680 cells in the floor; capacity not disclosed
Rangeover 300 miles (the 2017 promise was about 620)
Chargingover 500 kW on Supercharger V4; 15 to 80 percent in about 10 minutes on an 800 to 1,000 volt pack
Track endurance25 to 30 minutes at maximum power
Wheelbase111.2 inches
0–60 times shown1.0 s on a recorded test; 0.81 s live, not independently timed; 0.55 s claimed for the top spec, including a one-foot rollout

From Electrek and Wikipedia. That "one-foot rollout" is a drag-racing convention: the clock starts after the car has already moved a foot, which shaves time off every 0–60 figure that uses it.

The zeitgeist

The Roadster lands in a strange moment. Tesla's own future is the Cybercab, a car with no steering wheel, and here is Musk selling the last great car you drive yourself, built with parts from his rocket company while investors speculate about a Tesla and SpaceX merger. He said himself that he's "not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint." Electrek calls the jumps and flips "just a party trick" with no performance benefit, notes that a thruster plume throws debris tens of meters, and doubts the flying version will ever be practical. The 2017 reservation holders have been waiting almost nine years. And the first Roadster, the one Musk launched on a Falcon Heavy in February 2018 with a mannequin named Starman at the wheel, is still out there circling the Sun, which makes it the only Tesla Roadster so far to have actually flown farther than twenty feet.

About the pictures

The video is Tesla's own upload, played through YouTube's player only when you press play. The photograph at the top is Tesla's too: a frame from its own livestream, credited to Tesla by TechCrunch, which ran it the same night. I use it here to report on the event it shows, with credit, at reduced size, and I host the copy myself instead of pulling it from anyone's server. The diagram is mine, and the red illustration is an AI image I made with ChatGPT, labeled as such where it appears. Many outlets published striking photographs of the reveal, including Top Gear, Euronews, Ynet, Inc., and Mashable. Those belong to their photographers and publishers, so I link to them instead of copying them. Labeling someone else's photograph "fair use" doesn't make it so, and I'd rather send you to the people who shot them. If you own an image here and want it credited differently or removed, write to me.

entry.title: Pinebox started as a place to read mail in Alpine
entry.summary: Pinebox began in August 2026 as a tiny server for reading mail in Alpine. Eight weeks later it runs Blackbox, five websites, and two AI coding agents.
entry.content:
On August 21, 2026, I set up a small DigitalOcean server running Debian and named it Pinebox, after Pine, the University of Washington's old text-mode mail program, which I have used since 1993. The first thing I installed was Alpine, Pine's modern descendant, along with tmux and automatic security updates. Then I turned on the firewall. That was the whole plan: a quiet machine I could SSH into from any of my ThinkPads and read my Gmail in a text terminal.

For a few weeks it stayed that kind of place. On September 2 I imported my address book. On September 9 I set up S/MIME certificates for Alpine and curated a newsrc for reading Usenet. On September 12 I installed WordGrinder and Joe, two text-mode word processors, and the 1999 release of WordPerfect 8 for Linux, and made a ~/text folder for writing. A folder of poems followed at the end of the month. Pinebox was a writer's terminal with excellent email.

September 12 is also when I first talked to an AI on it, through a small chat script that logged every conversation. On September 29 I made a small repository of shell commands so every ThinkPad would reach Pinebox the same way. On September 30 everything changed: I installed git, the GitHub command line, and Claude Code, and that afternoon Claude and I made the first commit of Blackbox, the secretary that now runs my days. My own notes from that night include a to-do to bump the server to 1 GB of memory. It was already outgrowing its first size.

October is when the work moved in. Blackbox connected to Todoist, my Google calendar and inbox, and Upwork's new MCP server, with timers that renew its sign-ins twice a day, close my day at 11:45 PM, and push an encrypted backup every night. On October 4 I added a ~/projects folder, and Hill Mole moved in that day, followed by my firm's site on the 5th, my consulting site on the 6th, and my podcast's site on the 8th. On October 14 Claude set up Google's Lighthouse there to measure them all, and this weblog joined them tonight. On October 15 Node.js went in so OpenAI's Codex could join Claude Code, and the same day the server got a Google Places API key for local search work. Each new job came with its own requirements, and every one of them landed on a machine sized for reading email.

By tonight the numbers had caught up with the work. The server had one processor that sat mostly idle, 967 MB of memory with only 343 MB free, more than 400 MB already pushed into swap, and a disk 79 percent full. One Claude Code session alone was using 438 MB. Memory was the bottleneck, and two AI sessions at once meant everything slowed to a crawl. So I took a snapshot, powered it off, and resized it to two processors, 4 GB of memory, and an 80 GB disk, for about $24 a month. It came back with 3.2 GB free, no swap in use, the disk a quarter full, and every timer, backup, and sign-in intact.

Alpine is still there. When Blackbox drafts an email, it hands the draft to Alpine, and the message goes out only when I press Ctrl+X. The machine I set up to read email in a terminal still sends my email that way, with an AI secretary, two coding agents, and five websites living around it.

Update, October 16, 2026, 9:43 PM: Chris confirmed he has used Pine since 1993, so that detail is back in. Claude had cut an earlier version of the line because it had no source.

entry.title: Five live sites, five search labs
entry.summary: Chris Abraham runs five real websites that double as open labs for SEO, AEO, GEO, and AI search: what each one tests, and the one rule they all follow.
entry.content:
I run five websites, and every one of them is a real site doing a real job. This weblog is my lab notebook. The Chris Abraham Show site is the home of my podcast. Hill Mole is the spy novel I serialized on Movable Type starting in 2005. christopherabraham.com sells my consulting, and gerriscorp.com is my firm. Each of them is also a laboratory for search, for the old kind with ten blue links and for the new kind where ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Google's AI answers decide whom to name. The tools I use change every week, and these sites are where I find out what works before I sell it to anyone.

The rule is that nothing sneaky goes on any of them. No cloaking, no hidden text, no fake reviews, no doorway pages, no keyword stuffing, nothing that would get a site sandboxed if a Google engineer looked at it. Everything I test is something I would put on a client's site with my name on the invoice.

What they test is everything else. All five are static pages on GitHub Pages, built by Claude Code on my server, so a technical change that would take a WordPress plugin and a prayer takes a commit. On October 14 we ran a speed pass across the four older sites: Google Analytics, on the three that use it, now waits for the first scroll or tap, Chrome prefetches the next page when a reader hovers over a link, the robots files welcome the AI crawlers by name, and the podcast covers went to WebP. Every site has an llms.txt for AI assistants, structured data on every page, and IndexNow telling Bing about new pages the minute they go up. As of today, all four sites that run analytics use Google's Consent Mode, with no analytics cookies for visitors in Europe or for anyone whose browser asks not to be tracked, and Hill Mole, which runs no analytics at all, got a privacy page saying so.

Each site also tests something of its own. The podcast site has a page for every one of its 458 episodes, transcripts where Spotify made them, a glossary, and a hand-built back-of-the-book index with 1,774 headings, because an index is the kind of thing an AI can cite and a person can trust. Hill Mole wraps its untouched chapters in a reader's glossary, an index, sourced endnotes that catch the narrator in his mistakes, and an atlas, and keeps its 371 old Movable Type archive pages out of search so nothing appears twice. The two business sites publish guides and case studies with their own glossaries and site indexes, and their build refuses to publish a page that copies phrasing from the other site. This weblog is the newest, and it scores 100 on Google's Lighthouse for accessibility on every kind of page.

The lab results go somewhere. A small tracker I built asks the AI assistants the same sixteen questions and records whether my sites get named and cited, at about $1.60 a run, so I run it only when I mean to. What I learn on these five sites becomes what I do for clients, and what I can't make work here I don't sell.

It never submits anything. I paste the pitch myself, and that is how I want it.

Google is the other big one. My mail and calendar run on Google Workspace, and between Blackbox's own sign-in and the connectors in Claude Code, AI can now search my Gmail, read and draft messages, see my calendar, add events, and read and create files in my Drive. On October 15 I turned on the Google Places API in my own Google Cloud project, and Claude used it to pull the public Google listings for a local-services client and nine of its competitors. Google now runs more than fifty official MCP servers of its own, according to its April announcement, covering Gmail, Drive, Calendar, BigQuery, Maps, and much of Google Cloud.

Todoist is wired into everything: Blackbox treats it as the official task list, and Claude Code can read and change it too. GitHub runs through git and the gh command line, which is how five websites, including this one, get created, built, and pushed. Codex has its own short list, Screaming Frog and Gmail so far. ChatGPT and Claude.ai carry connectors on my accounts as well, and I haven't even catalogued those.

The next door is Basecamp. I have used Basecamp since 2006, starting with Abraham Harrison, and I am still on Basecamp 2. I am moving to Basecamp 5 so my AI tools can reach my projects. Basecamp's migration tool lets me choose which old projects come along, and with a paid Basecamp 5 account I keep Basecamp 2 at no cost; I just can't start new projects there. Basecamp 5 has a refreshed API, a command-line tool, agent Skills, and an official connector at mcp.basecamp.com/mcp that Basecamp says works in ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and Grok, included with every account.

What ties it together is MCP, the Model Context Protocol. Anthropic introduced it in November 2024 and donated it last December to the Agentic AI Foundation, under the Linux Foundation. A company builds one MCP server, and it works in Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, and Cursor alike. That is why the doors keep opening so fast.
